title: Stop Gluing Strings Together: f-strings Make Output Readable
excerpt: Build clear messages with f-strings: embed variables, format numbers and align columns without plus signs or str() calls.

headings.text: Write the Message With an f-string
Quotes and Curly Braces Inside f-strings

html:
Printing a message that mixes text and values is one of the first things every program does. The first way most people learn is to glue pieces together with +, and it gets ugly fast: quotes everywhere, spaces to remember, and a conversion for every number.

An f-string lets you write the message as a normal sentence and drop the variables straight into curly braces. It is the modern, readable way to build strings in Python.

The Glued-Together Way

Here is the version with +:

name = "Asha"
age = 31

print("Name: " + name + ", age: " + str(age))
Name: Asha, age: 31

It works, but you had to call str(age) and count the spaces by hand. Forget the conversion and Python complains with a TypeError, because it cannot join text and a number with +:

print("Name: " + name + ", age: " + age)
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

Write the Message With an f-string

Put the letter f right before the opening quote, then wrap any variable in {}:

print(f"Name: {name}, age: {age}")
Name: Asha, age: 31

Do you still need str() for the number? No, f-strings convert the value for you. And the braces can hold anything Python can calculate, not just a variable name: age + 1, or name.upper(), which turns the text into capital letters (upper() is a method, a built-in action you attach to a value with a dot):

print(f"Next year {name.upper()} will be {age + 1}")
Next year ASHA will be 32

While you are debugging (hunting for mistakes in your code), adding = after the name prints both the name and its value:

print(f"{age=}")
age=31

Format Numbers

After a colon inside the braces you can add a format specification, a short code that says how to show the value. What does :.2f mean? The .2 asks for two digits after the decimal point and the f means "show as a decimal number". Similarly, d means "whole number":

price = 1234.5678

print(f"{price:.2f}")
print(f"{1234567:,}")
print(f"{0.256:.1%}")
print(f"{42:05d}")
1234.57
1,234,567
25.6%
00042
  • :.2f rounds to two decimals.
  • :, adds thousands separators.
  • :.1% multiplies by 100 and adds a percent sign.
  • :05d pads a whole number with zeros up to 5 characters.

Line Up Columns

A number after the colon sets a minimum width. Use < to left-align and > to right-align within it. Each pair in the list, like ("pen", 3), is a tuple (a fixed group of values), and the loop splits each pair into item and quantity:

rows = [("pen", 3), ("notebook", 12), ("stapler", 1)]

for item, quantity in rows:
    print(f"{item:<10}{quantity:>4}")
pen          3
notebook    12
stapler      1

Each item gets 10 characters, padded on the right, and each quantity gets 4 characters, padded on the left, so the numbers line up neatly even though the words have different lengths. (The for loop simply repeats the indented line once for every row in the list.)

The Older format() Method

In older code you will often meet the format() method, which fills {} placeholders from the values you pass in:

print("{} is {} years old".format(name, age))
print("{:.2f}".format(price))
Asha is 31 years old
1234.57

It produces the same results as f-strings, but you have to look in two places to read one message. For new code, prefer f-strings. Which one should you use if you are reading older code? Both are correct, and there is no need to rewrite working code just to switch styles; simply know that the two forms are interchangeable.

Quotes and Curly Braces Inside f-strings

Two small situations trip people up. First, you often want to pull a value out of a dictionary (a collection of labelled values, where data['city'] looks up the value labelled "city") inside the message. Use a different kind of quote inside the braces than the one that wraps the string, which is a safe rule in every Python version:

data = {"city": "Pune"}
print(f"City: {data['city']}")
City: Pune

Second, what if you want to print a real curly brace character? Braces mean "insert a value" inside an f-string, so you double them to get an actual brace:

print(f"Use {{braces}} for placeholders, like {name}")
Use {braces} for placeholders, like Asha

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonFStrings.ipynb.

Summary

  • Start the string with f and put variables or expressions inside {}.
  • f-strings convert numbers to text automatically, so str() is not needed.
  • {value:.2f}, {value:,} and {value:.1%} control decimals, separators and percentages.
  • {text:<10} and {number:>4} set a width and align left or right.
  • {name=} prints the name and the value together, which is handy for debugging.
  • "...".format(...) does the same job in older code.
